**Meridian Freight cut its release cycle from three weeks to a day**

Meridian Freight moves about 4,000 truckloads a week, and nearly all of it runs on software the company writes itself. Until early last year that software shipped once every three weeks. Thursday nights. Four engineers on a bridge call, a rollback plan nobody had rehearsed, and a standing rule that no one deployed the week of quarter close.

"We weren't slow because we were careful," says Dana Okonkwo, who runs platform engineering. "We were careful because we were slow. Every release carried three weeks of changes, so every release was frightening."

Meridian adopted Conveyor in March 2024. The first six weeks were unglamorous — containerizing two Rails services, moving 140 database migrations behind feature flags, and getting the test suite from 41 minutes down to nine so a pipeline could actually gate a merge. No customer saw a thing.

The change showed up afterward. Meridian now deploys 19 times a week on average, mostly mid-morning, mostly by the engineer who wrote the change. Median time from merge to production is 22 minutes. Rollback is one click and takes about 90 seconds, which is the number Okonkwo says mattered most: once reverting got cheap, arguing about whether to ship got expensive.

Change failure rate fell from 14% to 4% over the following two quarters. The Thursday bridge call is gone. So is the quarter-close freeze — Meridian shipped a rate-quoting fix on the last day of Q4, at 3 p.m., with two people watching.

**Three weeks to one day: how Meridian Freight changed its release cadence**

Meridian Freight books roughly 4,000 truckloads a week, and almost all of that runs on software its own engineers write. Until early last year, that software shipped every three weeks, on a Thursday night, with four engineers on a bridge call and a rollback plan nobody had practiced. Quarter-close weeks were off limits by rule.

"People assume we were slow because we were careful," says Dana Okonkwo, who heads platform engineering. "It was the other way round. Three weeks of changes went out at once, so of course every release was frightening."

Conveyor went in during March 2024. The first six weeks were tedious: two Rails services containerized, 140 database migrations moved behind feature flags, the test suite cut from 41 minutes to nine so a pipeline could gate a merge without anyone waiting around. Customers noticed nothing.

What came after is the story. Meridian averages 19 deploys a week now, usually mid-morning, usually pushed by whoever wrote the change. Merge to production takes 22 minutes at the median. A rollback is one click and about 90 seconds, and that, Okonkwo says, is the number that mattered. Once reverting got cheap, arguing about whether to ship got expensive.

Over the following two quarters, change failure rate went from 14% to 4%. The Thursday bridge call is gone. So is the quarter-close freeze: Meridian shipped a rate-quoting fix on the last day of Q4, at 3 p.m., with two people watching.
